source.title: Ambiguous out-of-distribution generalization on an algorithmic task

record.file_problem: None; the full post and comments are present.
record.tranche_reason: The post tests delayed generalization on algorithmic group tasks, but changes the training-set construction to an ambiguous intersection and also measures complexity over training. This is a conceptual test rather than a direct reproduction of the usual grokking setup.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own experiments on one-hidden-layer MLPs trained on finite-group operations, including grokking rates, test accuracy over training, and complexity measures. Cited results from other work are not included as rows. Values visible only in plots are recorded only where the post also describes the result in text.
record.test_reason: The post reports its own runs of one-hidden-layer MLPs on finite-group operations. It observes memorize-then-generalize grokking in a new setting: under-specified training sets built from the intersection of two group tables. It also measures complexity measures over training. Its results bear on V1, V2 and V5, but it neither reproduces the original measure nor varies training-set size.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors present ambiguous out-of-distribution generalization as a concrete phenomenon: under-specified group data lead models to grok one of several completions, or neither. They find some evidence that simpler solutions, by LLC and circuit efficiency, are preferred, but cannot disentangle the two measures in this setting. They add that a model's choice is determined well before it shows in test behavior.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a one-hidden-layer MLP on finite-group operations, but trains on the intersection of two group tables rather than the usual iid subsample of one task. The post also uses full-batch gradient descent in its experiments and studies ambiguous completions.
record.method_sensitivity: The grokked solution varies across initialization seeds; outcomes also differ across group pairs and intersection datasets. The post notes that class imbalance may explain the no-grokking result for one group pair.

fits_no_version.finding: With an under-specified training set, seeds with fixed hyperparameters grok different valid completions or neither. S4 is strongly preferred over A4×Z/2Z.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When training data admit several generalizations, which one is grokked depends on initialization and is biased toward simpler solutions.

fits_no_version.finding: Final LLC is associated with which group is grokked, and stays high or falls in non-grokking models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower LLC predicts which of several generalizing solutions is grokked.

fits_no_version.finding: Moving grokked models to an ambiguous intersection set partially ungroks 7–8% of them while intersection accuracy stays perfect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A shift to under-specified data can undo prior grokking.

record.problems: The post says the proportions in the 100-model experiment are low-confidence because grokking is rare and the sample is small. Several complexity findings are qualitative or plot-based; the authors report that LLC and training loss are highly correlated and cannot be disentangled. No causal intervention tests whether weight decay produces the observed solution preference.
record.rows_left_out: No additional outcome rows retained. The training-Jacobian discussion is not a direct test of the listed grokking versions; the post itself says its late-training blow-up may be a numerical-instability artifact.

untested.parts: Whether the grokking delay grows as the training set shrinks. The delay is not quantified.
Identification of a generalizing circuit forming gradually, and removal of memorizing components.
All of it: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm switch.
All of it: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Causal role of weight decay, the critical dataset size, and ungrokking below that size.
Whether one well-specified task yields the same algorithm across runs. Only a footnote spot-check of regrokked parameters touches this.
All of it: optimizer or numerical controls are not tested.

missing.what: Perturbation sensitivity: Gaussian weight perturbations at checkpoints show the model decides its solution well before test accuracy reveals it, with a sensitivity bump near epoch 600.
Total variation of logits over epochs 2500–3000: grokking models lock in their solution, while many non-grokkers keep oscillating.
Spot-check: regrokked parameters differ from the originally grokked ones but share many neurons in the same irreps. The authors say this is not representative.
Models trained on an iid subset of S5 consistently grok, a baseline grokking result.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post, not peer-reviewed. V6 links were removed throughout: seed-dependent choice among valid completions of under-determined data is not the same as different algorithms for one task. The S4 experiments use about 4,000-parameter models and the S5 experiments about 80,000. Training is full-batch gradient descent with a constant learning rate.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not establish that the delay grows as the training set shrinks: it does not compare time-to-grokking across training-set sizes.
It measures LLC and other progress measures, but does not identify a generalizing circuit forming gradually or show memorizing components being removed.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm transition is tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The post does not manipulate weight decay to test causality, or test a critical dataset size or the predicted ungrokking below it.
The post studies different outcomes across initialization seeds in its tested group tasks; it does not compare architectures or a broad range of hyperparameters.
It does not test whether grokking disappears when adaptive-optimizer instabilities or softmax floating-point limits are controlled.
